evals.prompt: We're at Loftwell (workflow automation software, about $9M ARR). We signed 62 partners over the past 14 months - roughly two-thirds resellers, the rest digital agencies - and exactly 7 have ever registered a deal. Enablement is me, half-time. The good news is our direct sales org has a really solid enablement library already: a 60-slide pitch deck, an objection-handling doc, the rep onboarding video series, and a competitive teardown. I want partner enablement stood up in the next 8 weeks. Where do we start and what does the whole plan look like?
evals.expected_output: An interview-first engagement that gathers deadline, ambition and effort-ceiling answers, presents and ranks the three sequencing approaches before designing, recommends the minimum-viable first-deal path, and treats the existing direct-sales library as unusable unchanged.
expectations: Asks clarifying questions one at a time rather than batching several into a single message.
Asks for the date the result must land by, whether the user wants a one-off win or a compounding asset, and the effort ceiling, before proposing any plan.
Presents exactly three sequencing approaches - minimum-viable first-deal path, certification-first launch, and comprehensive up-front curriculum - before designing anything.
States the ranking of those three approaches out loud rather than implying it through list order.
Recommends the minimum-viable first-deal path as the default.
Waits for the user to pick a sequencing approach before building out the roadmap sections.
Treats the existing direct-sales pitch deck, objection doc, rep onboarding videos and competitive teardown as unusable by partners in unchanged form, and says so explicitly.
Names adaptation per role and partner type - not better distribution or a portal upload - as the fix for the direct-sales library.
Calls for at least one partner-only asset that has no direct-sales equivalent, such as a margin calculator, co-brandable collateral, or deal-registration mechanics.
Defines the first-deal path as the minimum knowledge, access, and actions a partner needs to register one qualified opportunity.
Attaches a total partner-hours figure to that first-deal path.
Keeps the first-deal path within roughly a working day of partner time.
Labels everything beyond the first-deal path as explicitly post-first-deal rather than as a prerequisite.

evals.prompt: Our CEO came back from a customer advisory board convinced we need a certification program. Company is Arvexa - document workflow software, about 40 channel partners, mostly small resellers of 8 to 30 people. What he wants: three certification levels, a mandatory 90-day curriculum every partner completes, three multiple-choice exams, and no partner may register a deal until they have passed all three. Live by the end of next quarter. Help me build it.
evals.expected_output: A redesign that moves certification behind the first deal, tests whether certification is warranted at all, replaces multiple-choice gating with a capability check, and surfaces the burden and brand exposure a marketed credential carries.
expectations: Warns that placing mandatory certification before the first deal is a known failure pattern, with stalled partners and collapsed activation as the outcome.
Notes that the partners who finish a pre-deal gauntlet tend to be those with idle bench capacity rather than those with customers.
Recommends moving certification to a post-first-deal milestone instead of a pre-registration gate.

Tests whether certification is warranted at all against conditions such as customers checking credentials before buying, an unvalidated partner damaging customers, or the need for a defensible gate for tiers, co-sell priority, or lead routing.
States that certification is not a default component of a partner program.
Offers a capability check inside onboarding - a live pitch or demo pass - as the alternative for a small or young program.
States that multiple-choice knowledge exams are the weakest signal and are acceptable only for entry-level product literacy.
Recommends a hands-on lab or practical assessment as the minimum for any credential that gates economics.
Requires each certification level to gate something economic - tier status, discount level, MDF eligibility, lead routing, or co-sell priority - or not exist.
Flags that a vendor-marketed credential is a public capability claim needing legal or brand sign-off.
Notes that the credential is hard to withdraw once partners advertise the badge.
Sizes the certification burden numerically as hours per person times people required times exam fees, against the economic payoff the partner sees.
Raises certified-headcount requirements as a wall for partners of 8 to 30 people.

evals.prompt: Pinecrest Data here - we run a referral-only partner program. 130 partners, all consultancies and boutique advisory shops who pass us names. None of them implement anything; we do 100% of delivery ourselves and that is not changing. I sketched an enablement plan with five tracks: partner sales rep, solutions architect, delivery/implementation consultant, partner marketer, exec sponsor. I marked the delivery track as phase 2 for next year since nobody needs it yet. Review the plan and tell me what to build first.
evals.expected_output: A revised audience map that deletes the tracks no role in this base fills, names them as deleted rather than deferred, and orders the surviving tracks by build effort against what each unblocks.
expectations: Removes the delivery/implementation consultant track from the plan entirely rather than deferring it to a later phase.
Names that track explicitly as deleted in the audience map, with the reason that the partner base contains no delivery consultants.
Warns that a track parked as a later phase returns as scope nobody budgeted.
Applies the same existence test to the solutions architect / pre-sales track, given a referral-only base that neither demos nor implements.
Keeps a track for every customer-facing role that does exist in this base.
Sizes referral-partner depth as roughly a 30-minute product overview plus a clean handoff mechanic.
Orders the surviving tracks by build effort against what each one unblocks, not by importance alone.
States that ordering out loud rather than leaving it implied by row order.
Builds the partner sales rep track first.
Expresses build effort in orders of magnitude such as an hour, a week, a quarter, or a standing job.
Cites the risk of spending months of enablement built for a partner profile that does not exist in the base.

evals.prompt: I have $40,000 approved for partner enablement this year and a hard ceiling of one week of build time per asset - anything bigger I cannot staff. Company is Northbound Logistics Software, 28 resellers. I need a ranked build list, most cost-effective first, with a cost against each line so I can show finance exactly what we are cutting. On the table: sales play and battlecard, deal registration walkthrough, co-brandable pitch deck, demo script plus a self-guided demo environment, a pre-sales technical track, and an implementation/delivery track with certification.
evals.expected_output: A build order expressed in effort magnitudes against what each item unblocks, with no currency attached, the over-ceiling items struck rather than deferred, and the starved item named with its promotion condition.
expectations: Refuses to attach a currency figure to any item in the build order.
Gives the reason for that refusal: a price goes stale faster than the ordering it was meant to justify.
Expresses each item's build effort as an order of magnitude - an hour, a week, a quarter, or a standing job.
Pairs each item's effort with what that item unblocks rather than reporting effort alone.
Ranks the deal-registration walkthrough at or near the top on effort-to-outcome ratio, sized at about an hour of screen recording.
Places the sales play and battlecard first or second, on the grounds that the items beneath it have nothing to sell without it.
Deletes the demo environment, the pre-sales technical track, and the implementation/certification track from this cycle given the stated one-week-per-asset ceiling.
Says explicitly that those items are struck, rather than listing them as a later phase.
States the ranking out loud rather than implying it through row order.
Names the demo environment as the item this efficiency ordering starves.
Gives the condition that would promote the demo environment anyway - deals stalling at the demo stage, or partners pulling a vendor rep onto calls.
Does not present the $40,000 figure as the basis for the ordering.

evals.prompt: Median time from partner signature to first closed deal is 143 days at Halcyon Grid (network monitoring, 51 partners). Last year it was 96. Leadership is treating this as a training problem and has asked me to rebuild the curriculum. Before I spend a quarter on that, what is actually going on and what do I do?
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis that works the three candidate causes in order, isolates which one is actually an enablement fault, checks the cheap disqualifying items first, and withholds a curriculum rebuild until the cause resolves.
expectations: Refuses to treat an inflated time-to-first-deal as automatically an enablement fault.
Names three candidate causes - the enablement minimum being too large, partner manager overload, and partners signed without qualification - and works them in that order.
States that only the first of those three is an enablement problem.
Checks the size of the mandatory pre-selling path before proposing any curriculum rebuild.
Checks whether a partner economic case was ever made.
Routes a recruiting or program-structure cause to the sibling partner program-design skill rather than solving it inside the enablement roadmap.
Works the cheapest disqualifying check before the expensive one.
Notes that trending above roughly 90 days is the commonly cited rebuild signal for time-to-first-deal.
Flags that time-to-first-deal bands come from PRM-vendor or channel-consultancy sources with undisclosed methodology and are directional rather than measured.
Asks whether the metric counts closed-won or first deal registration before benchmarking against any band.
Does not commit to rebuilding the curriculum before the diagnosis resolves.

evals.prompt: Board meeting in five weeks. Our partner academy shows 78% course completion and 212 certificates issued across 44 partners, average quiz score 86%, and training CSAT of 4.4 out of 5. I want a slide that says our enablement investment is paying off. What is the strongest version of that slide, and what am I missing? Company is Verrick Systems, B2B security tooling.
evals.expected_output: A correction that platform metrics only evidence the lower evaluation levels, plus the cohort comparison, data join, and role-level coverage view needed to evidence that enablement actually worked.
expectations: States that completion rates, quiz scores, and training satisfaction reach only Kirkpatrick Levels 1 and 2.
Identifies that Levels 3 and 4 require deal-registration and CRM data joined to the learning-platform data.
Names the trained-versus-untrained partner cohort comparison as the measurement that separates enablement having happened from enablement having worked.
Specifies the comparison dimensions: partner-sourced opportunities, time-to-first-deal, and win rate.
Requires unified partner identity across the learning platform, portal, and CRM before that comparison is possible.
Warns that attribution breaks the moment those systems stop sharing a partner ID.
Rejects the 212 raw certificate count as a capability measure and requires certification coverage by role per partner instead.
Gives the failure a raw count hides: a partner holding many sales certificates and no technical ones.
Calls for a certified-but-inactive list of partners who completed training and produced no pipeline.
States that completion above roughly 60-70% is described as strong yet proves nothing without activation.
Attaches a reliability flag to any benchmark band cited, noting the figures are PRM-vendor sourced with undisclosed methodology.
Warns against citing vendors' own circulating cohort claims, such as certified partners earning multiples more or structured onboarding closing first deals 2-3x faster, as evidence.
Recommends running the user's own cohort comparison instead of citing published figures.
Does not present the 78% completion rate or the 86% quiz average as evidence that enablement worked.

evals.prompt: Partner portal logins are down 41% quarter over quarter at Brightmoor Tech. We have 380 assets in there covering absolutely everything, downloads are flat, and even our top 10 partners barely log in. My read is that partners just are not motivated, so I want to add points, badges and a leaderboard to pull engagement back up. Sanity check me before I brief the vendor.
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis ordering access friction ahead of motivation, naming the asset volume as a content-dump failure, and converting the request log into a ranked build backlog instead of adding gamification.
expectations: Diagnoses access friction - passwords, login flow, slow interface, poor findability - before partner motivation.
Notes that single-sign-on portals see measurably higher engagement.
Identifies 380 assets as the documented content-dump failure rather than a strength.
Recommends curating ruthlessly: identify the small fraction of assets that drives revenue and retire the rest.
Recommends an asset-request path so partners can ask for what they do not see.
Treats the asset-request log as the build backlog, ranked by request count against the build effort each request implies.
Gives the shape of that ranking, such as a repeatedly requested one-pager outranking a single request for a lab.
Checks asset origin - whether the assets were recycled from direct-sales enablement - as a content-fit question before treating the problem as distribution.
Reads falling engagement as a leading indicator of commercial decline rather than as a standalone metric.
Treats low adoption of one specific asset as a signal about that asset: update, reposition, or retire it.
Checks whether partners are rebuilding assets themselves, which signals a co-brandability or fit failure rather than a distribution failure.
Does not recommend gamification as the primary fix.

evals.prompt: I run partner programs at Copperline Group. Until now it has been software resellers, but we just acquired a company with 140 franchised service locations plus a dealer network of 60 independent dealers. I have been told to extend our existing partner training program to cover them. Our current program is role-based tracks, an online academy, and an annual certification tied to tier status. What changes?
evals.expected_output: A design that adds the train-the-trainer layer, switches certification to per-site mandatory coverage with its compliance weight, reshapes front-line content, and names what carries over unchanged.
expectations: Adds a train-the-trainer layer where the brand trains the franchisee or general manager, who then trains their own staff.
States that this layer is structural in franchise and dealer networks rather than an optional addition.
Flags that brand-standard certification in franchising carries legal or compliance weight that B2B partner certification does not.
Changes certification coverage to per-site and mandatory for the franchise locations.
Contrasts that per-site coverage with B2B's per-organization certified-headcount thresholds.
Designs front-line content as short, motivating micro-content with competitive literacy for hourly staff.
Contrasts that with B2B partner reps as independent economic actors who need a margin case.
Notes that franchisors can contractually mandate training completion while B2B vendors can only incentivize it.
Keeps role segmentation before building anything as unchanged across both worlds.
Keeps the academy or learning platform as the delivery backbone in both worlds.
Does not apply the B2B margin-case framing to hourly front-line staff.

evals.prompt: Leadership wants our certification program to look like AWS's. Specifically: Advanced tier needs 6 certified individuals, Premier needs 25 with at least 10 at professional level, plus launched-project counts with a minimum MRR. We have 34 partners, median size 12 people, and I would like to publish the new tier requirements in six weeks. Draft the requirements. Company is Saltwick Analytics.
evals.expected_output: A response that refuses to transplant a hyperscaler structure, flags its staleness, separates individual from organizational instruments, contrasts composite against checklist validation, and hands threshold design to the tiering skill.
expectations: Warns that large-vendor program structures are revised roughly annually and must be re-verified against the vendor's own current program documentation before any detail is cited.
Advises against copying a large vendor's structure, on the grounds that its partner counts and budgets are orders of magnitude larger than this program's.
Flags a 6-certified and 25-certified headcount requirement as a wall for partners with a median size of 12 people.
Notes that at least one major cloud program added a small-business designation after partner feedback on exactly this headcount problem.
Recommends a lighter track for small partners before headcount requirements wall them out.
Distinguishes individual accreditation from organizational competency as two different instruments.
States that the organizational designation, not the individual credential, is the instrument that gates tiers and co-sell eligibility.
Contrasts weighted composite scoring, where strength in one category partially offsets another, against discrete checklist validation, where every control is satisfied individually.
Gives the criterion for choosing between them: composite for flexibility and partner-friendliness, checklist for defensibility and consistency.
Recommends free-and-short credentials at the individual entry level, with expensive validation reserved for the organizational level.
Hands the tier threshold design - where the bar sits in the ladder, measurement windows, gameability checks - to the partner-tiering sibling skill rather than setting it here.
Sets an expiry or renewal cadence per credential level rather than issuing permanent credentials.
Pairs any increase in recertification cadence with delta-training on what changed rather than full re-examination.

evals.prompt: I have three weeks to produce an enablement plan for Kelso Interactive's channel, 47 partners. I already know what is wrong - I talk to our three best partners constantly and they have told me exactly what they need: better competitive positioning and a demo environment. I would rather not burn a week on interviews. Write me the plan.
evals.expected_output: A needs assessment that widens the sample to include inactive partners or mines existing artifacts, produces a gap document ranked by impact per unit of fix effort, and pilots before scaling.
expectations: Pushes back on designing the plan from the three best partners alone.
Specifies interviewing 5-10 partners deliberately split between active and inactive ones.
States that inactive partners are the more valuable half, because they explain why the program failed them.
Offers a fallback when interviews are impossible: mining joint business plans, QBR notes, the portal's asset-request log and search queries, support tickets, and win/loss notes.
Produces a gap document mapping each enablement component from current state to desired state.
Carries evidence, impact, and fix effort per gap in that document.
Ranks gaps by impact per unit of fix effort rather than by impact alone.
Explains that ranking by impact alone promotes the quarter-long gaps and buries the hour-long ones.
Sizes the demo environment as roughly a few weeks of work and competitive positioning as roughly a day or two that rides along with the sales play already being written.
Concludes that competitive positioning ships before the demo environment even though the demo environment ranks higher on impact.
Plans a pilot cohort with selection criteria, success criteria, a feedback loop, and a scale trigger before rolling out broadly.
Recommends socializing the near-final roadmap through a partner advisory council before public launch, rather than using the council to generate the first draft.

evals.prompt: Two things. First, I need the actual partner battlecard and a 20-question certification exam by Friday for Windmere Cloud's new reseller program. Second, our plan is to put every prospective partner through the full product and sales training during the evaluation period, before they sign the reseller agreement, so that we only ever sign partners who are already trained. 19 partners in the pipeline. Go.
evals.expected_output: A scope correction that declines to author the training artifacts, moves training behind signature while keeping the economic case before it, and assigns single accountable ownership plus per-asset owners and refresh dates.
expectations: Declines to write the battlecard copy and the exam questions, and states that those are downstream deliverables built from the roadmap.
Describes what the roadmap does instead: it sequences and gates.
Moves product, sales, and technical training to after signature.
Keeps the partner value case and partnership economics before signature.
Names training a partner with no economic reason to invest as the documented 'no value proposition for the partner' pitfall.
States that partners are rational economic actors who ration selling time across competing vendors.
Requires every track to answer what the partner gets economically before it lists any content.
Names a single accountable owner for the enablement roadmap.
Keeps that single ownership even where content creation stays distributed across product marketing, channel ops, or a training team.
Names fragmented ownership across those teams as a documented failure pattern.
Budgets an enablement track for the vendor's own channel organization - partner managers, channel sales, solutions engineers.
Assigns an owner and a review or refresh date to every asset class.
Stops at an approval gate, finalizing nothing without the user's explicit approval of the assembled spec.
